paragraphs: Swamiji once spoke about Patanjali, the great Indian philosopher who lived around fourteen hundred years before Christ. Patanjali gathered up the facts, evidence and research on the human mind that had piled up over the ages, and built on all that earlier experience. The world, Swamiji reminded his Western listeners, is very old. Some in the West were taught that society only began with the New Testament, some eighteen centuries ago. That might be true of the West, he said, but certainly not of the whole world.

While lecturing in London, Swamiji had a friend, a brilliant and well-read man, who loved to argue with him. One day, after trying every argument he had, the friend suddenly demanded: if India had such great rishis, why hadn't they come over to teach England?
Swamiji's answer was quick. There was no England for them to come to back then. Were they supposed to preach to the forests?

He also recalled a remark from Ingersoll, the American freethinker. Ingersoll told him that if he had come to preach in America fifty years earlier, he would probably have been hanged, burnt alive, or chased out of the villages with stones.
So, Swamiji concluded, there is nothing unreasonable in believing that civilisation was flourishing in India fourteen hundred years before Christ.
learn: What we call 'the beginning' often just means where our own textbook starts. Before you dismiss another culture's history, check the timeline. A quick, calm reply can win more than a long argument.
